title: Bits, Bytes & Number Bases
oneLiner: Every number in a computer is bits -- binary, decimal, and hex are just three readings of the same bit pattern.
keyTakeaway: A byte is 8 bits, and each bit is a power of two (128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1) -- decimal is those powers added up wherever there's a 1. Hex is a shorthand on top: every group of 4 bits becomes exactly one hex digit (0-9, then A-F for 10-15), which is why hex is the readable way to write raw bytes (like colors, #FF9900) instead of binary.
explanation: Decimal (base 10) uses ten digits and place values that are powers of ten -- present because we have ten fingers, not because it's fundamental. A computer only has two states per wire (on/off), so it uses base 2: each bit is a power of two, and a number is just "which powers of two are switched on, added together." A byte is 8 bits, so it can represent 2^8 = 256 distinct values -- 0 through 255 unsigned (read as never negative). Hex (base 16) exists purely as a human-friendly shorthand for binary: because 16 = 2^4, every 4 bits maps to exactly one hex digit with no remainder, so a full byte is always exactly 2 hex digits (0x00 to 0xFF; the 0x prefix is how code marks a number as hex). Toggle bits below and watch all three representations update together -- and flip on "signed (two's complement)" to see how negative numbers are represented without a separate minus-sign bit: the leftmost bit doubles as a sign indicator, and negative values are the bit pattern you'd get from "invert every bit, then add 1" to the positive version.
